column4: The section names root م ل ك and its dictionary sense *milāk*, what keeps a wall cohesive; here a wall about to collapse is set upright, فَأَقَامَهُ. In the same ayah the travelers' request for food is refused, joining withheld human aid to structural repair.
The section's *nasta'in* (root ع و ن) means asking for aid; Zülkarneyn says فَأَعِينُونِي بِقُوَّةٍ and asks people to lend strength for a barrier, turning aid into a structure that will stand.
The section pictures a weak person supported at the sides; Musa asks that Aaron strengthen his back, اشْدُدْ بِهِ أَزْرِي, making bodily support the means to carry a task.
The promise سَنَشُدُّ عَضُدَكَ بِأَخِيكَ gives Musa his brother as strength at his arm, a close bodily counterpart to the section's wavering traveler held up by others.
The section's dictionary gloss calls *qiyām* a pillar/support; Lot longs for a رُكْنٍ شَدِيدٍ, a strong refuge-pillar, when he cannot protect his guests alone.
The section's *mustaqīm* carries bodily uprightness as well as a straight route; this ayah sets one who walks face-down against one who walks سَوِيًّا on a straight path.
The section's weak traveler depends on two people; this parable depicts a man unable to act and wholly dependent on his master, then contrasts him with one on a straight path.
In the battle scene, rain removes hardship, strengthens hearts, and steadies feet, وَيُثَبِّتَ بِهِ الْأَقْدَامَ; divine aid is pictured as making people physically firm.
The promise وَيُثَبِّتْ أَقْدَامَكُمْ makes God's response to support a concrete one: He firms the feet of those who support His cause, echoing the section's aid that lets a person stand and walk.
The section's roots ع و ن (aid) and ه د ي (guidance) meet here: whoever holds fast to God is guided to a straight path, فَقَدْ هُدِيَ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ.
The section's roots ع و ن and ه د ي join aid to guidance; this ayah joins holding fast to God, وَاعْتَصَمُوا بِهِ, with His guiding people to a straight path.
The section describes help as what one leans on; here the believer holds to an unbreakable handhold, الْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَىٰ, an explicit image of dependable support.
Turning oneself to God and holding fast to the firmest handhold, اسْتَمْسَكَ بِالْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَىٰ, gives the section's bodily leaning a direct image of secure reliance.
Moses names the strain of travel, نَصَبًا, and asks his companion for food; the ayah gives a concrete Quranic traveler whose journey has left him spent and in need.
After watering the women's flock, Moses withdraws into shade and prays, إِنِّي لِمَا أَنزَلْتَ إِلَيَّ مِنْ خَيْرٍ فَقِيرٌ. A traveler who has helped others then states his own need before God.
The section's root ه د ي includes a wavering walk and the request for guidance; here a confused person is lost on earth while companions call him to guidance, الْهُدَى, and back to the right way.
The section's dictionary form *hedy-i hasen* describes calm, good walking; the servants of the Merciful are described as يَمْشُونَ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ هَوْنًا, walking gently on earth.
The command وَاقْصِدْ فِي مَشْيِكَ asks for measured walking, closely matching the section's calm, unhurried gait after support.
The section's dictionary example has a tree standing on its roots; this good tree has أَصْلُهَا ثَابِتٌ, a fixed root, and branches rising upward, making rooted stability visible.

The section begins with a mount that tires or is injured; this ayah shows the ordinary service that such a failure interrupts: livestock carry people's burdens to distant places otherwise reached only with hardship.
The section's traveler needs both ground to walk on and guidance; God makes earth مَهْدًا, a resting-place, and puts paths in it so people may be guided.
Earth is made مَهْدًا and routes are laid through it; this joins a supporting surface with a way to travel, the two needs embodied in the section's stranded walker.
The earth is spread as a بِسَاطًا and people are given paths through it; the verse makes the ground itself a support for movement along ways.

The section opens with a mount that fails its rider; here riders settle upon the backs of ships or animals, لِتَسْتَوُوا عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِ, showing the bodily support the failed mount can no longer give.

The section's mount has stopped carrying its traveler; this ayah names reaching one's needs on livestock and being carried on them, وَعَلَيْهَا وَعَلَى الْفُلْكِ تُحْمَلُونَ, the support in its working state.
This ayah names livestock as a source of many benefits and food; 23:22 adds that people are carried on them, completing the mount-as-support image in the section.
This ayah states وَعَلَيْهَا وَعَلَى الْفُلْكِ تُحْمَلُونَ: people are carried on livestock and ships, the direct image of a mount supporting a traveler.

The section's root ع و ن names aid and helping; وَتَعَاوَنُوا calls believers to support one another in goodness and reverence, extending the two people holding up the weak traveler into shared action.
The section's *nasta'in* is a request for aid; this command says وَاسْتَعِينُوا بِالصَّبْرِ وَالصَّلَاةِ, naming patience and prayer as supports to seek.
Moses tells his people, اسْتَعِينُوا بِاللَّهِ وَاصْبِرُوا; the section's request for help is here joined to patience while facing hardship.
After the brothers' false account and bloodied shirt, Jacob says وَاللَّهُ الْمُسْتَعَانُ; the section's root ع و ن appears as help sought from God when human reports cannot be relied on.
The section names root ع و ن for aid and names the Merciful in its opening; this ayah says وَرَبُّنَا الرَّحْمَٰنُ الْمُسْتَعَانُ, joining its Rahman and help-seeking language.
Among commands to treat others well, this ayah names both وَالصَّاحِبِ بِالْجَنبِ and وَابْنِ السَّبِيلِ, joining a companion at one's side with the traveler who needs care.
The command to give the wayfarer his due, وَابْنَ السَّبِيلِ, supplies a social counterpart to the section's stranded traveler: his need creates a right to others' help.
The wayfarer, وَابْنِ السَّبِيلِ, is explicitly among those eligible for alms, making communal resources a form of aid for the traveler in need.
The section's tree stands on its roots; the contrary tree is uprooted, اجْتُثَّتْ, with مَا لَهَا مِن قَرَارٍ, no stable place to remain.

The section's dictionary wording says the good walk is not rushed like a defeated person; at Uhud the believers climb away without turning back, إِذْ تُصْعِدُونَ وَلَا تَلْوُونَ عَلَىٰ أَحَدٍ, the explicit fleeing gait that bounds the calm image.

The section's q-w-m dictionary sense is erect standing; here the usurer's rise is likened to one stumbling in a demonic seizure, لَا يَقُومُونَ إِلَّا كَمَا يَقُومُ الَّذِي يَتَخَبَّطُهُ, a distorted opposite of steady uprightness.
The section's calm, good gait is bounded by the arrogant walk condemned here, وَلَا تَمْشِ فِي الْأَرْضِ مَرَحًا.

The command not to walk arrogantly, وَلَا تَمْشِ فِي الْأَرْضِ مَرَحًا, opposes the section's measured, unhurried walk; this ayah adds that human strength cannot pierce earth or reach the mountains in height.
The section's q-w-m image concerns what stands securely; this account contrasts a town still قائم with one reaped down, وَحَصِيدٌ, making standing and collapse neighboring conditions.
The section pictures a person leaning on human helpers, while this Judgment Day boundary says no patron can avail another, لَا يُغْنِي مَوْلًى عَن مَّوْلًى شَيْئًا, and none will be helped.
Against the section's bodily help from others, this account of the Day of Recompense says no soul controls anything for another and الْأَمْرُ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِلَّهِ.
The section's image depends on help from another person; this warning about the Day of Recompense says no soul can avail another and وَلا هُمْ يُنصَرُونَ, setting a limit on human aid.

The people ask for a barrier against the attackers, فَاجْعَلْ بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَهُمْ سَدًّا; adjacent 18:95 supplies the distinct contribution of asking for strength to build it, linking the need for protection to requested aid.

The section's tree example emphasizes standing on roots; this next ayah says the good tree yields its fruit continually, تُؤْتِي أُكُلَهَا كُلَّ حِينٍ, showing what rooted stability sustains (14:24 gives the fixed-root image).
Moses asks for a helper from his family, وَاجْعَل لِّي وَزِيرًا مِّنْ أَهْلِي; linked 20:31 states what this support should do, strengthen his back.
Moses names Aaron as the requested helper, هَارُونَ أَخِي; linked 20:31 makes the bodily support explicit as strengthening his back.
Moses asks to share his work with Aaron, وَأَشْرِكْهُ فِي أَمْرِي; linked 20:31 explains the support's effect, strengthening his back for the task.
The verse pairs emigration with those who gave shelter and aid, وَالَّذِينَ آوَوا وَنَصَرُوا; it depicts travelers being received and supported after leaving home.
This verse describes poor emigrants expelled from homes and property who seek God's bounty; it places people made vulnerable by travel and displacement within a community's responsibility.
Those who received emigrants love them and prefer them over themselves, وَيُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِمْ; the verse shows people becoming another's support.
The answer about charitable spending includes وَابْنَ السَّبِيلِ among its recipients, giving the section's traveler in need a place in a list of people others must support.
The verse commands giving the wayfarer his due, وَابْنَ السَّبِيلِ, a repeated Quranic formulation of material support for a traveler.
The poor described here are restricted in God's way and لَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ ضَرْبًا فِي الْأَرْضِ; their inability to move through the land makes need and immobility meet in one scene.
When unable to give the requested material help, the addressee is told to answer with قَوْلًا مَّيْسُورًا; this adds a humane response for the person whose need cannot be met.
The command وَأَمَّا السَّائِلَ فَلَا تَنْهَرْ gives a direct boundary on how to receive someone who asks, like the section's person seeking aid.
This ayah establishes a known right in people's wealth; 70:25 identifies the asker and deprived as recipients, completing the link to the section's person seeking aid.
This ayah identifies the asker and deprived, لِلسَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ, as those with a known right in wealth, making aid available to people in need.
The prayer asks not to be burdened beyond capacity, لَا تُحَمِّلْنَا مَا لَا طَاقَةَ لَنَا بِهِ, then asks God for victory; it voices dependence and need for help from a place of human weakness.
The weak, sick, and resource-less are excused from setting out; this names bodily weakness and inability to travel as a concrete boundary on movement.
The blind, lame, and sick are excused from battle; the explicit عَرَج, lameness, gives a bodily mobility counterpart to the section's disabled mount and weak walker.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are provided لِتَرْكَبُوهَا; this identifies the normal ride whose exhaustion or injury strands the section's traveler.
The ayah names ships and livestock as what people ride, مَا تَرْكَبُونَ, the travel support whose failure opens the section's image.
God provides livestock لِتَرْكَبُوا مِنْهَا; the verse identifies animals as the means carrying a journeyer before the section's mount becomes unable to move.
The animals are made manageable, and مِنْهَا رَكُوبُهُمْ; the section's exhausted mount is a reversal of this stated riding benefit.
Mountains keep the earth from shaking, أَن تَمِيدَ بِهِمْ, while routes are made through it; the verse joins a stable ground to paths for travelers.
The mountains prevent the earth from shaking, أَن تَمِيدَ بِكُمْ, and the verse names rivers and paths; stable ground and a route are provided together.
The section names q-w-m and gives the dictionary gloss *qiyām* as support; the Kaaba is made قِيَامًا لِّلنَّاسِ, a communal support.
The section's q-w-m dictionary branch glosses *qiyām* as a prop or support; the divine name الْقَيُّومُ presents God as the one who sustains all, a broader scale of that support.
The section's q-w-m dictionary branch glosses *qiyām* as support; الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ repeats the name of the one who sustains, in a shorter declaration than 2:255.
The section hears bodily uprightness in *mustaqīm*; the purpose لِيَقُومَ النَّاسُ بِالْقِسْطِ uses the q-w-m family for people standing up for justice, extending uprightness into a public stance.
The section names q-w-m as the family behind standing upright; كُونُوا قَوَّامِينَ بِالْقِسْطِ applies that standing to a sustained commitment to justice.
The section's q-w-m image includes bodily straightness; the command كُونُوا قَوَّامِينَ لِلَّهِ applies the root to standing firmly as witnesses for justice.
The command وَقُومُوا لِلَّهِ قَانِتِينَ places upright bodily standing inside worship, joining the section's movement from serving God to seeking aid.
The section names root ق و م in *mustaqīm* and makes uprightness bodily; Zakariya is قَائِمٌ يُصَلِّي in the sanctuary when the angels call him, joining standing posture with worship.
The section's q-w-m family carries bodily standing; this ayah tells worshippers to remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides, naming the body's changing postures.
The servants of the Merciful spend the night سُجَّدًا وَقِيَامًا; the verse places standing bodily posture within worship, one side of the section's 1:5–1:6 movement.
The section names root ق و م in *mustaqīm* and makes uprightness bodily; this ayah names remembrance of God while قِيَامًا وَقُعُودًا وَعَلَىٰ جُنُوبِهِمْ, standing, sitting, and lying on sides.
Allah holds the heavens and earth so they do not cease, يُمْسِكُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ أَن تَزُولَا; this enlarges the section's image of support that prevents collapse.

The section's dictionary entry calls the heart the body's *milāk* or support; this ayah says hearts find rest, تَطْمَئِنُّ الْقُلُوبُ, through God's remembrance, an inner steadiness rather than bodily structure.
In the cave, the Prophet reassures his companion, لَا تَحْزَنْ إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَنَا; God then sends tranquility and support, joining companionship to aid in distress.
God supports the Prophet through believers and brings their hearts together; the verse makes people a source of backing, as in the section's two companions supporting one walker.
After believers are warned that enemies have gathered, they say حَسْبُنَا اللَّهُ; their reliance on God under threat parallels the section's aid sought when human strength is insufficient.
People sailing through a storm call to God to save them, دَعَوُا اللَّهَ مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ; this is another traveler dependent on a conveyance who seeks aid when it fails.

The section names root ه د ي for guidance and ق و م in *mustaqīm*; God calls to the Home of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path, picturing guidance as leading a traveler to a destination.
The section names root ه د ي for guidance; here speakers ask why they should not rely on God after He has guided them to their ways, وَقَدْ هَدَانَا سُبُلَنَا, joining reliance to direction.

The section names ق و م in *mustaqīm* and describes a person leaning on support; here the command فَاسْتَمْسِكْ بِالَّذِي أُوحِيَ إِلَيْكَ is followed by the claim that the addressee is on a straight path, joining holding fast to the way.
The section names roots ع ب د and ق و م in its worship and straight-path wording; Jesus says to worship God and calls it a straight path, فَاعْبُدُوهُ هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ.
The section names roots ع ب د and ق و م in its worship and straight-path wording; the command أَنِ اعْبُدُونِي is identified as the straight path, هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ.
The section names roots ع ب د and ق و م in its worship and straight-path wording; Jesus says worship is the straight path, فَاعْبُدُوهُ هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ.
The section names roots ع ب د and ق و م in its worship and straight-path wording; Jesus says worship is the straight path, فَاعْبُدُوهُ هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ.
God commands, فَاعْبُدْنِي وَأَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ; the section's q-w-m family and worship theme meet in a command to worship and establish prayer.
The section names root ه د ي for guidance; this ayah asks who guides people in the darknesses of land and sea, مَن يَهْدِيكُمْ, making guidance a need of travelers crossing difficult terrain.
Moses is told to travel by night and make for his people a dry path through the sea, فَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ طَرِيقًا فِي الْبَحْرِ يَبَسًا; guidance here opens a route for travelers in danger.
When the sea blocks the fleeing people, Moses says إِنَّ مَعِيَ رَبِّي سَيَهْدِينِ; trust in God and the promise of guidance answer a traveler's apparent dead end.
The section hears uprightness in the q-w-m family of *mustaqīm*; this ayah says the Qur'an guides to أَقْوَمُ, what is most upright, joining guidance to uprightness.
